interactions.label: What makes the right adrenal vein more hazardous than the left during adrenalect

params.question: What makes the right adrenal vein more hazardous than the left during adrenalectomy?

answers.text: It is longer than the left and prone to torsion during mobilisation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The right adrenal vein is actually shorter, not longer. Its brevity is precisely what makes it hazardous — there is almost no length of vein to work with before the IVC.

answers.text: It receives tributaries from the inferior phrenic artery, complicating dissection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The inferior phrenic artery is one of three arterial sources to the adrenal gland, but arteries and veins are separate structures. The danger of the right adrenal vein is its venous drainage pattern, not its arterial connections.

answers.text: It is short and drains directly into the inferior vena cava, leaving almost no margin for error

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The right adrenal vein is short and empties directly into the IVC. A tear during dissection causes rapid, difficult-to-control venous haemorrhage. The left adrenal vein, by contrast, is longer and drains into the left renal vein, giving the surgeon more working room.

answers.text: It runs posterior to the kidney, making laparoscopic visualisation difficult

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While the adrenal glands are retroperitoneal and sit above the upper pole of the kidney, the danger of the right adrenal vein is its short course directly into the IVC, not its position relative to the kidney.

overallFeedback.feedback: The right adrenal vein is short and empties directly into the IVC, unlike the longer left adrenal vein that drains into the left renal vein. This venous asymmetry is a key surgical hazard during adrenalectomy.
Correct! The short right adrenal vein drains directly into the IVC — a tear here causes rapid, hard-to-control haemorrhage with very little margin for error.

interactions.label: Why must catecholamine excess be excluded biochemically before performing a biop

params.question: Why must catecholamine excess be excluded biochemically before performing a biopsy on an adrenal mass?

answers.text: Because elevated catecholamines indicate metastatic spread to the adrenal gland

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Catecholamine excess indicates a phaeochromocytoma (a primary adrenal medullary tumour), not metastatic disease. Metastases from lung, breast, or kidney are assessed separately.

answers.text: Because biopsy of an unsuspected phaeochromocytoma can trigger a life-threatening catecholamine crisis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mechanical stimulation of a phaeochromocytoma during biopsy can provoke massive catecholamine release, causing severe hypertension, tachycardia, and potentially fatal cardiovascular collapse. Biochemical screening with plasma or urinary metanephrines is mandatory before any invasive procedure.

answers.text: Because catecholamine-secreting tumours are always benign and do not require biopsy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Approximately ten per cent of phaeochromocytomas are malignant. The reason for excluding catecholamine excess before biopsy is patient safety during the procedure, not the tumour's biological behaviour.

answers.text: Because catecholamines interfere with histological staining, rendering the biopsy sample uninterpretable

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The concern is patient safety, not sample quality. A needle entering an unsuspected phaeochromocytoma can trigger a catecholamine storm with haemodynamic collapse.

overallFeedback.feedback: Needling an unsuspected phaeochromocytoma can trigger massive catecholamine release, causing life-threatening hypertension and cardiovascular collapse. Always measure plasma or urinary metanephrines before performing a biopsy on any adrenal mass.
Correct! Biopsy of an unsuspected phaeochromocytoma can provoke a fatal catecholamine crisis — biochemical exclusion is a mandatory safety step before any needle passes into an adrenal mass.

params.question: In pre-operative preparation for phaeochromocytoma, what is the consequence of starting beta-blockade before establishing alpha-blockade?

answers.text: It delays catecholamine clearance, prolonging the duration of surgery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Beta-blockade does not affect catecholamine clearance. The danger of reversing the blockade order is haemodynamic, not pharmacokinetic.

answers.text: It causes excessive hypotension from dual receptor blockade, making anaesthesia unsafe

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The concern is actually the opposite — hypertension, not hypotension. Without prior alpha-blockade, beta-blockade removes the vasodilatory counterbalance while alpha-mediated vasoconstriction continues unchecked.

answers.text: It increases the risk of adrenal haemorrhage by altering glandular blood flow

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Adrenal haemorrhage is not related to the order of receptor blockade. The risk is a systemic hypertensive crisis from unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction.

answers.text: It leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, risking a severe hypertensive crisis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Beta-receptors mediate vasodilation and heart rate control. Blocking them first removes this counterbalance while alpha vasoconstriction continues unopposed, potentially triggering a severe and life-threatening hypertensive crisis. Alpha-blockade must run for 10–14 days before surgery; a beta-blocker is added only afterwards if tachycardia persists.

overallFeedback.feedback: Starting beta-blockade first blocks vasodilatory beta-receptors while alpha vasoconstriction continues unopposed, risking a severe hypertensive crisis. The correct sequence is alpha-blockade for 10–14 days, then a beta-blocker only if tachycardia persists.
Correct! Beta-blockade before alpha-blockade removes the vasodilatory counterbalance, leaving alpha vasoconstriction unopposed — a potentially fatal sequencing error.
